headline: Niantic Fleet Whispers: Fluke Sliding Off the Grass and Onto the Reefs Now
subhead: A neap tide is softening the current through Twotree and the Race, and the drift boats are cashing in on fluke, sea bass, and a stripers-after-dark pattern.
body_markdown:
I was leaning on the rail at the bait shop Tuesday morning when one of the Waterford boat mates came in for a second load of squid strips and said something that stuck with me: "They ain't in the grass no more, they're all on the humps." He meant the fluke, and he wasn't wrong. We flagged this a week or so back — said the back-bay fluke would start pushing out to inlet mouths and ocean-adjacent reef structure as the water warmed through July, and that's exactly what's happening from Niantic Bay out through Twotree Island Channel right now.

The drift boats working out of Niantic and Waterford have been putting together solid fluke counts in 35 to 45 feet off the reef edges around Twotree and out toward Hatchett Point, with the better fish coming on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the drop. Pink and white Gulp on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a squid strip, has been the go-to combo — nothing fancy, just a slow drag right along bottom where the structure breaks up the current. New London's reading around 69 degrees, which is a touch cool compared to the western Sound, but that's actually helping keep these fluke locked onto structure instead of scattering into open water. Sizes have been a mixed bag — plenty of 16 to 18 inchers getting tossed back, but every drift is putting at least one or two keepers in the 20 to 22 inch range over the rail. It's not a banner week, but it's a dependable one, and dependable counts for a lot in late July.

Sea bass have been the more consistent story on the same structure. Guys working ledge and rockpile around Hole-in-the-Wall and the Twotree drop-offs are finding steady numbers of sea bass in the 14 to 17 inch class, with the occasional heavier fish mixed in — nothing quite like that 28-inch, five-pound brute that got weighed in over toward Plum Gut, but that tells you the size class is out there on this eastern end of the Sound if you find the right piece of bottom. Green crab and squid combo on a two-hook bottom rig, fished tight on structure with just enough weight to hold in the current, has been the standard. Porgies are riding shotgun on the same drops — smaller stuff mostly, but a good bend-your-rod distraction between fluke drifts, and they'll eat the same squid strips you're already carrying.

Striped bass are the tougher conversation this week. The shallow water from here down through the western Sound has stayed warm enough that the keeper-class fish have gone almost entirely nocturnal — dawn, dusk, and after dark around the rips and structure is where the action's concentrated, and daytime trips have been mostly quiet unless you're working deep current breaks. Black Point and McCook Point have both given up fish after sundown to guys drifting live eels or working large soft-plastic swimbaits through the current seams, but you need to be out there in that low-light window, not mid-morning. A few schoolies are still showing on top around the Niantic River mouth on the early outgoing, chasing peanut bunker, but the bigger fish want the dark and the moving water together.

Bluefish haven't really made their presence felt out here yet the way they have further west — the bunker-driven blitzes tearing up the beaches from Belmar into Raritan Bay haven't pushed this far east in any real numbers. I wouldn't be shocked if that changes as bunker schools keep working the coast, but for now blues in this zone are more incidental — a few slammers mixed into the fluke drift here and there, nothing you'd plan a trip around.

The bigger structural story this week is the neap tide. We're coming off the first-quarter moon, and that means softer current through the rip-dependent stretches — Twotree Channel, the approach toward the Race — over the next several days. That's actually good news if you're working bucktails or bottom rigs, because the window of fishable current widens out instead of being crammed into that one violent hour of max tide. It also means slower, more finesse presentations are going to outfish the heavier gear for the time being — lighter jigs, slower retrieves, less horsepower needed to hold bottom.

Looking ahead, if the current stays soft through the week like it should on this neap cycle, I'd keep working the fluke and sea bass pattern on structure with lighter tackle — that's the higher-percentage play right now. For stripers, I'd plan around the tide and the clock together: fish the last two hours of light into full dark on the outgoing around Black Point or the river mouth, and have eels or a bulky swimbait ready. If the wind stays out of the south and holds calm like it's been, I don't expect much to change fast — just keep showing up on the structure and let the tide do the rest of the work.
